# 2 Kings Chapter 6 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 227r–228r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2KI_006_page_001.jpg, 2KI_006_page_002.jpg, 2KI_006_page_003.jpg

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** The sons of the prophets said to Elisha, "The place where we dwell before you is too small for us.

**2** Let us go to the Jordan, and let each of us take a beam from there, and let us make a place there for us to dwell." He said, "Go."

**3** Then one of them said, "Please be willing to go with your servants." He answered, "I will go."

**4** So he went with them, and when they came to the Jordan, they began to cut down trees.

**5** But as one was felling a beam, the iron axe head fell into the water. He cried out, "Alas, my master! It was borrowed!"

**6** The man of God said, "Where did it fall?" When he showed him the place, Elisha cut a stick and threw it in there and made the iron float.

**7** He said, "Pick it up." So he reached out his hand and took it.

**8** Now the king of Aram was at war with Israel, and he took counsel with his officers, saying, "At such and such a place shall be my camp."

**9** But the man of God sent word to the king of Israel, saying, "Beware of passing that place, for the Arameans are going down there."

**10** So the king of Israel sent to the place of which the man of God told him. He warned him repeatedly, and he was on his guard there, not once or twice only.

**11** The heart of the king of Aram was greatly troubled over this matter, and he called his officers and said to them, "Will you not tell me who among us is for the king of Israel?"

**12** One of his officers said, "None, my lord the king; but Elisha, the prophet who is in Israel, tells the king of Israel the very words you speak in your bedroom."

**13** He said, "Go and find where he is, that I may send and seize him." It was reported to him, "He is in Dothan."

**14** So he sent horses and chariots and a great army there. They came by night and surrounded the city.

**15** When the servant of the man of God rose early and went out, behold, an army with horses and chariots was surrounding the city. His servant said to him, "Alas, my master! What shall we do?"

**16** He said, "Do not be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them."

**17** Then Elisha prayed and said, "O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see." And the LORD opened the eyes of the servant, and he saw — and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha.

**18** When the Arameans came down against him, Elisha prayed to the LORD and said, "Please strike this people with blindness." So he struck them with blindness, according to the word of Elisha.

**19** Then Elisha said to them, "This is not the way, and this is not the city. Follow me, and I will bring you to the man you seek." And he led them to Samaria.

**20** When they entered Samaria, Elisha said, "O LORD, open the eyes of these men that they may see." The LORD opened their eyes and they saw — and behold, they were in the midst of Samaria.

**21** The king of Israel said to Elisha when he saw them, "Shall I strike them down? Shall I strike them down, my father?"

**22** He answered, "You shall not strike them down. Would you strike down those whom you have taken captive with your sword and your bow? Set bread and water before them, that they may eat and drink and return to their master."

**23** So he prepared a great feast for them, and when they had eaten and drunk, he sent them away and they went to their master. And the Aramean raiding bands came no more into the land of Israel.

**24** After this, Ben-hadad king of Aram gathered his entire army and went up and besieged Samaria.

**25** There was a great famine in Samaria as they besieged it, until a donkey's head was sold for eighty pieces of silver, and a quarter of a kab of dove's dung for five pieces of silver.

**26** As the king of Israel was passing along the wall, a woman cried out to him, "Help, my lord the king!"

**27** He said, "If the LORD will not help you, how can I help you? From the threshing floor or from the winepress?"

**28** Then the king said to her, "What is your trouble?" She answered, "This woman said to me, 'Give your son, that we may eat him today, and we will eat my son tomorrow.'

**29** So we boiled my son and ate him. The next day I said to her, 'Give your son, that we may eat him.' But she has hidden her son."

**30** When the king heard the words of the woman, he tore his garments — now he was passing along the wall — and the people looked, and behold, he had sackcloth beneath on his body.

**31** Then he said, "May God do so to me and more also, if the head of Elisha the son of Shaphat remains on him today!"

**32** Now Elisha was sitting in his house, and the elders were sitting with him. The king sent a man ahead, but before the messenger arrived, Elisha said to the elders, "Do you see how this murderer's son has sent to take off my head? When the messenger comes, shut the door and hold it fast against him. Is not the sound of his master's feet behind him?"

**33** While he was still speaking with them, the messenger came down to him and said, "This disaster is from the LORD! Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?"

---
## SOPHIA's Council Notes

Chapter 6 contains three distinct episodes united by the theme of seeing and not seeing: the floating axe head (a small miracle of provision), the blinding and unblinding of the Aramean army (divine sight versus human blindness), and the siege of Samaria (where the king's eyes are opened to the horror of cannibalism). Elisha's instruction to feed the blinded enemy rather than slaughter them (vv.22-23) is one of the Hebrew Bible's most remarkable ethical moments — mercy as military strategy. The chapter ends in theological crisis: the king has been secretly wearing sackcloth (faith under pressure), but the cannibalism shatters his endurance. His question "Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?" sets up the prophetic answer in chapter 7.

---
## Disagreement Log

### V.5 — "Alas" vs. "Oh no"
- **EMET/LOGOS:** "Alas"
- **PNEUMA:** "Oh no"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Alas" — preserves the Hebrew exclamation *ahah* with appropriate gravity. "Oh no" is too colloquial for the formal register of the consensus text.

### V.12 — "servants" vs. "officers"
- **EMET:** "servants" (literal *avadim*)
- **LOGOS/PNEUMA:** "officers"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "officers" — while *avadim* literally means "servants," in the context of a military king consulting his staff, "officers" better conveys the actual role. EMET's literalism is noted.

### V.22 — Rendering the ethics of the command
- **EMET/LOGOS:** "Would you strike down those whom you have taken captive with your sword and your bow?"
- **PNEUMA:** "You don't execute prisoners of war you didn't even capture yourself."
- **SOPHIA ruling:** Follow EMET/LOGOS — the rhetorical question form preserves the Hebrew syntax and Elisha's persuasive strategy. PNEUMA's paraphrase, while clear, loses the force of the question.

### V.25 — "dove's dung" vs. "seed pods"
- **EMET/LOGOS:** "dove's dung" (literal *chireyyonim*)
- **PNEUMA:** "seed pods"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "dove's dung" — the literal reading should be preserved in the text, with the possible botanical identification noted. The shock value of the Hebrew is deliberate.

### V.33 — Speaker identity
- **EMET:** Ambiguous (messenger speaks king's words)
- **LOGOS:** The king arrives and speaks
- **PNEUMA:** The king speaks
- **SOPHIA ruling:** Render as the messenger arriving and the king speaking, following the most natural reading of the Hebrew transition. The ambiguity is noted but resolved for clarity.

---
*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
